title: SHA-256 PoW kernel compiled for sm_75 (Tesla T4): shipped vs optimised
how: Kaggle notebook on a Tesla T4 (40 SMs, 1590 MHz, CUDA 13.0 / nvcc 13.0.88), built and run by src/sass/kaggle_t4_sass.py

measured.shape: 33,554,432 nonces x 5 reps, one tail block per nonce, T4
measured.correctness: both kernels verified word-for-word against a CPU compression before timing (difficulty 0 so every nonce is a hit)

what_was_changed: the shipped kernel builds the message block in a local unsigned char[64]: zero 64 bytes, write the nonce, patch the length, then read all 16 words back through load_be32 - 96 bytes of local memory per thread
the optimised kernel builds W[0..15] in registers; for the sha256 family (u32 nonce, one tail block) W1=0x80000000, W2..W14=0 and W15=bit length are constant for a challenge and are not rebuilt
rotations use __funnelshift_r so ptxas emits SHF; the hit test is shared so only the compression path differs
negative_result: ILP does not help on this kernel: 1, 2 and 4 nonces per thread measure 2,390 / 2,412 / 2,407 MH/s. The SM is issue-throughput-bound, not latency-bound, so ILP=1 is right - it also uses 40 registers instead of 64/128, i.e. full occupancy.
why_the_shipped_number_varies: 1,348-1,749 MH/s across runs because the 96-byte stack frame is local-memory traffic whose cost depends on L1/L2 state. The register-only kernel measures the same 2.4 GH/s every run.
caveat: the shipped kernel supports both the decimal-nonce (fast/slow) and u32-nonce (sha256) families with a runtime branch; the optimisation is specific to the sha256 family. The decimal path can be specialised the same way but the digit conversion still costs, so it was not measured here.
not_done: the optimised kernel is not wired into src/cuda/cuda_sha256.cu; that needs a GPU to validate the library path end to end, which this repo's test suite can do on a T4 runner.
